questions.question: What does errors.New do, and when is it enough?
questions.title: Creating a simple error with errors.New
questions.direct_answer: `errors.New(text)` creates a non-nil error whose content is the supplied message. It is enough for a fixed, self-contained failure that callers only need to report or propagate. Use formatting, wrapping, a sentinel, or a custom type when the failure needs context or machine-readable identity.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic error construction and the boundary between a message and a stable error identity.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling errors.New repeatedly and expecting equal messages to create equal errors.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish a one-off descriptive error from a package-level sentinel.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `errors.New` creates an error from a fixed text message.
Each call returns a distinct error value, even for the same text.
Use it for simple failures with no dynamic fields.
Declare it once when callers need a reusable sentinel identity.
Do not make program decisions by comparing error strings.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`errors.New` is the simplest standard way to create an error from a text message. The returned value implements `error`, and printing it produces exactly that text. I use it when the failure has a fixed explanation and the caller does not need structured fields or an underlying cause.

For example, a small validator can return `errors.New("name is required")` when an empty name is invalid. The caller checks whether the result is nil, then displays or propagates the error. There is no need to define a new type just to carry one stable sentence.

Every call to `errors.New` creates a distinct value, even if two calls receive identical text. If callers need to recognize a category, the package should declare one reusable variable such as `var ErrClosed = errors.New("closed")` and return or wrap that same value. Callers can then use `errors.Is`.

It is not the best tool for dynamic context such as an item ID, because string concatenation becomes noisy and still does not preserve a cause. `fmt.Errorf` handles formatted context and `%w` wrapping. A custom type is better when callers need fields. I choose `errors.New` only when a plain message fully represents the failure.

sections.title: A message is the smallest useful error
sections.content:
The implementation returned by `errors.New` is intentionally simple: it stores text and supplies an `Error` method. That is valuable because many local failures need nothing more. Extra types would add ceremony without improving a caller's decision.

The moment identity matters, creation strategy changes. A package-level variable gives all returns one stable target. The moment data matters, a structured type gives fields names and types. Error design should grow only to match the information contract.

questions.question: Why should a sentinel error be declared once and reused?
questions.title: Stable sentinel errors
questions.direct_answer: A sentinel error is a package-level error value that represents one documented condition, such as `ErrNotFound`. Declaring it once gives callers a stable identity to test with `errors.Is`; constructing the same message repeatedly creates different values and loses that identity.

interviewer_intent.testing: Stable error categories, wrapping, and API compatibility.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Recreating an error with the same message at every failure site.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that an exported sentinel is a long-term contract and should represent a useful caller decision.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A sentinel is one shared error value for a named condition.
Conventionally its exported name begins with `Err`.
Return it directly or wrap it with `%w` to add context.
An exported sentinel becomes part of the package API.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A sentinel error is one reusable value that names a specific condition. A package might declare `var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")`. Every code path representing that condition returns the same value or an error that wraps it, so callers have a stable target independent of wording.

For example, `FindUser(42)` can return `fmt.Errorf("user 42: %w", ErrNotFound)`. The message contains useful local context, while `errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound)` remains true. A handler can translate that category to HTTP 404 without parsing the sentence or importing an internal database error.

Repeating `errors.New("not found")` inside the function does not work as a category. Each call produces a distinct value, and matching by `err.Error()` is fragile because messages change, gain prefixes, or become localized. Identity and presentation have different jobs.

The boundary is API design. Exporting `ErrNotFound` promises callers that this condition is detectable, which can constrain future implementation changes. I use a sentinel when a small category is enough for a meaningful branch. If callers need data such as which field failed or what limit was exceeded, I prefer a custom type and `errors.As`.

sections.title: Concept guide · Stable sentinel errors
sections.content:
A useful error often needs two layers. The inner sentinel says what class of event occurred; the outer wrapper says where it happened in this call. `errors.Is` follows the wrapping relationship to recover the category, while ordinary formatting shows the whole explanation.

This model also creates a review checkpoint: only conditions the caller can act on deserve public identities. Implementation-specific failures can be translated into a package's own category instead of leaking a dependency's contract.

sections.title: Context around a stable category
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[ErrNotFound sentinel] --> B[wrap with user ID]
  B --> C[return error]
  C --> D[Display: user 42 not found]
  C --> E[errors.Is]
  E --> F[Match ErrNotFound]
```

questions.question: Are two errors.New values equal when their messages match?
questions.title: Error text does not define identity
questions.direct_answer: No. Each call to `errors.New` returns a distinct error value, so two separately created errors are not equal just because their messages match. Reuse a sentinel for a stable category, and use `errors.Is` when that sentinel may be wrapped.

interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate direct equality and errors.Is with both distinct values and a reused sentinel.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Equal message text does not make two error values identical.
Every `errors.New` call returns a distinct value.
Comparing `Error()` strings is not a stable classification strategy.
Reuse one sentinel when identity matters.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Two separate calls to `errors.New` do not create equal errors, even when the input text is identical. The text is what a person reads; it is not a unique type or category. The errors package deliberately returns a distinct value for each call.

For example, `errors.New("closed") == errors.New("closed")` is false. Creating a fresh `errors.New("closed")` in a test and comparing it with the function's result is therefore also false. Comparing the two `Error()` strings might pass, but it couples control flow to presentation text.

If `closed` is a condition callers must recognize, I declare `var ErrClosed = errors.New("closed")` once and return that exact value. When a function adds context with `fmt.Errorf("send message: %w", ErrClosed)`, direct equality no longer reaches the inner value, but `errors.Is(err, ErrClosed)` does.

Not every error needs an identity. A one-off error that will only be displayed can remain a fresh value. I introduce a sentinel only for a documented branch that callers can handle, use a custom type for structured details, and never infer semantics by searching the message string.

sections.title: Identity and wording answer different questions
sections.content:
Messages are allowed to become more descriptive as an error moves through the program. Classification must survive those edits, so it needs something other than text. A shared value supplies identity; a wrapper preserves its relationship to added context.

Tests should mirror the public contract. Check `errors.Is` for a promised sentinel, `errors.As` for a promised type, and message fragments only when the exact presentation is itself the feature being tested.

sections.title: What each comparison can prove
sections.content:
| Check | Same fresh message | Same sentinel | Wrapped sentinel |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `err1 == err2` | false | true | false |
| `errors.Is(err, target)` | false | true | true |
| `err.Error() == text` | may be true | may be true | usually false after context |
